{"docket_number": "76-577", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1976", "first_party": "Zacchini", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Company", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "Ohio Supreme Court", "argued": ["1977-04-25T05:00:00Z"], "question": "

Do the First and Fourteenth Amendments immunize the Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co. from damages for its alleged infringement of an entertainer's state-law right of publicity?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

Hugo Zacchini performed a "human cannonball" act, in which he was shot from a cannon into a net 200 feet away. A free-lance reporter for Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co. recorded the performance in its entirety without consent and it aired on the nightly news. Subsequently, Zacchini sued Scripps-Howard, alleging the unlawful appropriation of his professional property. Ultimately, the Ohio Supreme Court ruled in favor of Scripps-Howard. While recognizing that Zacchini had a cause of action for the infringement of his state-law right to publicity, the court found that Scripps-Howard was constitutionally privileged to include in its newscasts matters of public interest that would otherwise be protected by the right of publicity, absent an intent to injure or to appropriate for some nonprivileged purpose.

", "conclusion": "

No. In a 5-4 opinion delivered by Justice Byron R. White, the Court held that Scripps-Howard's constitutionally privileged free speech did not extend to broadcasting Zacchini's entire performance without his permission. Noting that Zacchini's interest in the case was similar to a patent or copyright, in which he was seeking to obtain the benefit of his work, the Court emphasized that the broadcast of an entire act was categorically different from reporting on an event in so far as it posed a substantial threat to the economic value of the performance. "Wherever the line in particular situations is to be drawn between media reports that are protected and those that are not, we are quite sure that the First and Fourteenth Amendments do not immunize the media when they broadcast a performer's entire act without his consent," wrote Justice White. Justice Louis F. Powell, Jr., joined by Justices William J. Brennan, Jr., and Thurgood Marshall, dissented, arguing that the recording was genuinely treated as news and as such Scripps-Howard was constitutionally privileged. Justice John Paul Stevens also dissented.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in 76-577, Zachini against Scripps Howard. Thank you. Thank you. I'm John Lansion, arguing for the petitioner. In this case, we are here by virtue of the question involving the applicability of freedom of the press in the First Amendment, as it is and has been applied to the right of publicity as expressed by the Ohio State Supreme Court. In our case, a public performer, a man who has an act known as the human cannonball, was performing at a local fair, and I believe the critical facts in this case revolve around the way the news media ended up putting his performance on its news show. And that is, a newspaper reporter, a freelance reporter, went to the fair and made an inquiry of Mr. Zachini concerning the filming of his act and was told specifically that this privilege was rejected and that he did not wish his act to be filmed by the reporter. The reporter returned and spoke to the news manager and was told, by way of affidavit, to go out and film the act. And indeed he did. And the act takes 15 seconds for Mr. Zachini to complete. That is his only professional show. That is the entirety of his performance. He shot out of a cannon and travels several hundred feet in the air, lands in a net. In 15 seconds, that's the end of it. It is dramatic. It is unusual. And that's why I take it that he's been able to sell this act around the country and make a living. The Supreme Court of Ohio, in response to our motions, stated that there is indeed a right of publicity that inheres in a professional entertainer's act, that he has a property right to govern how, when, and where his performance is published. Did they identify it as a property right? A proprietary interest, I believe, Your Honor. That's not... Is that in the syllabus? I... Well, they call it... The syllabus, yes. ...has a right to the publicity value of his performance. Yes. The invasion of privacy in syllabus one, Your Honor, refers to the benefit of the name and likeness of another being subject to liability to the other for invasion of his privacy, and then they refer to this right of the publicity value in his performance. I think in the language they say proprietary interest, but in any event, it is a substantial right that an individual has. A private individual who seeks to become an entertainer. And they say that this right of publicity inheres in his performance. Now then, they go, they take a step further, and in the third syllabus they say, the First Amendment, however, allows the press to report in a newscast matters of legitimate public interest. What would you call this? Reporting or reproducing? I would call this a verbatim reproduction. They went in with a TV camera, and they filmed everything he had to show. The only reason that it occurred, I would suggest, is because it was a 15-minute act, and he specifically rejected their proposal to put it on their news shelf. And we've been told a good many times in Ohio cases, when they come here, that the law of the case is the syllabus, the headnote, not the opinion. Is that binding on, is that law of Ohio? Yes, it is, Your Honor. Now, is that particular concept of Ohio law binding on this court in a First Amendment case? I don't think so. I think that this court must look behind the bare syllabus, the three paragraphs that summarize what happened, and determine what the facts were. We have accepted it, I think, tacitly, as binding for some purposes. That's why I focus on the proposition. Is it binding on this court when we're dealing with a First Amendment case, which is not the First Amendment not being the exclusive property of the courts of Ohio? I think for that purpose, that is true. I was suggesting that to determine what actually happened and what the court is saying, the court must take into consideration the facts. But I think in syllabus three is what we're dealing with. Mr. Lanci, in that respect, I notice that the Court of Appeals opinion, looking at page 828, in paragraph three, I guess these are headnotes, and that's the syllabus, are they? No, that is not. The only binding... That court says, a performer's act is the product of his talent, as such it is property, entitled to the same protection under the common law as any other property right. Now, does that holding have any significance in this case in light of the absence of some similar statement from the syllabi? I don't think so, Your Honor, because in the Court of Appeals, the headnotes are not the law of the case in Ohio. So we may ignore that and concentrate on the syllabi of 123. No, I am contending that it is a property right. I believe it is. What I'm suggesting is, certainly it isn't stated as explicitly by the Supreme Court in the syllabi as it's stated by the Court of Appeals. That is true, Mr. Justice Brennan. Well, is there any significance in that the Supreme Court didn't use the same phrase? I don't think so. I don't see any particular significance to it. I think that they've created a substantive right, a tort remedy, the invasion of the right of publicity. To state it in terms of property, personality, or realty, I don't think is the intent of using the word property or proprietary interest. It has a right to the publicity value of his performance. Yes. It is explicable, only if they mean by that that that's tantamount to a property. Yes, I think they do mean that, but I don't think they've stated it specifically in the Supreme Court syllabus. Would you give me the difference between the right of publicity and the right of privacy? Yes, Justice Marshall. The right of privacy is the right to have those matters kept away from the public which the public has no right to know about. For example, in the Firestone case, I believe that the right of privacy was involved because the reporter cited the fact that a counterclaim had been dismissed when it dealt with adultery on the part of Mary Alice Firestone. And it also has, the right of privacy prohibits those in the media from, or anyone else, from giving a false light to facts which are known to the public. Where the right of privacy, the right of publicity is almost the opposite. An entertainer wants to be in front of the public. He wants to be publicized and advertised. And I'm sure he, Mr. Zucchini, would have appreciated the fact that they mentioned on their show or showed a picture of him and said, Hugo Zucchini is going to be shot out of a cannon. I mean, he'd probably have loved to have Channel 5 put that on every half hour. So he would get more people out there to enhance the value of his act. Then he does advertise. Oh, yes. Yes, he does. Mr. Lancione, would you be here if there had been just a still photograph of him in mid-flight rather than the 15-second tape? No, Your Honor, I would not. What's the difference? I think that the news media has a right to publicize in an entertainment section, for example. They can advertise to the public that there's an entertainment section on their 11 o'clock news show, and they can tell about everyone of import or of little import who is performing in and about the area where their readers and listeners are concerned about. But what we have here is the taking of an entire total performance. Let me change my question a little bit. Suppose this performance had been in a public square and you used to have one in Cleveland. Suppose it had been there. Free of charge. Would it make any difference? No, I do not. I do not believe that the media has the right under the First Amendment privileges, as they've been enunciated and interpreted, to publish, to capture and publish a performer's entire act. I think that is protected. His act in its entirety becomes his peculiar property. And I do not think that under any circumstances, unless there is a waiver, which the Supreme Court of Ohio declared there was not, that the news media can come in and say, we call it news, and therefore, we can do whatever we want to. To what extent, however, is he subject to what the entrepreneur, the empresario, does or does not do? Well, if it was a private matter between the people who have contracted for him to come in and perform, I don't think we're dealing with that. I think that he, whatever arrangement he makes, he may waive some right for the person who has purchased his act. Well, let me read you what is at the bottom of performances, the program at the Kennedy Center here. The taking of photographs and the use of recording equipment are not allowed in this auditorium. This is by the management of the Kennedy Center. Does this reflect at all on the situation? Suppose the, that statement were just the reverse, that the taking of photographs is permissible in the Kennedy Center. Well, I think that if it did say that, and it probably, there was probably nothing said to the persons who came into the Burton, the Geauga County Fair in Burton, Ohio. Or in the Kennedy Center. That's right. I don't think the news media can come in under the guise of the First Amendment and capture any performer's complete act, unless there is a waiver. There may be a waiver in the circumstances that you're discussing. If the performer knows that there will be persons in their recording his performance, he may be held to waive. But, news programs don't only take 15 minutes or half an hour. Some programs take an hour. There are special news shows. And the, the thing, the point that puts this in an appalling perspective is that any time the news media calls it news, under the third syllabus, they are granted an indefeasible immunity and privilege. would you be here if Ohio had just said, well, under our law there is no right in publicity or no right, no property right or any other kind of a right in this man? Well, I don't think I... You don't think the First Amendment gives it to him? No, I don't think... So that's a matter of Ohio law. I think it's a matter of Ohio tort law like anything else. What if, what if the Ohio court had said, well, we recognize that there is a right, a property right of publicity or whatever you want to call it, but as a matter of Ohio law, the press has a limited privilege of reporting it and they have not exceeded it in this case. suppose that's what the, what the, the third syllabus had said. You wouldn't be here either, would you? If there was no interpretation of the First Amendment, I would not be here. Well, then how do we know what they, how they act? If you just look at the syllabus here, it doesn't say, does it, whether it's a First Amendment, they took a First Amendment approach, whether they thought the First Amendment required the privilege or whether they are just announcing a matter of Ohio law. we are permitted, uh, Mr. Justice White, to look into the body of the decision to interpret the syllabus of the case and on page A13, the court clearly states that the effect of this holding and that of New York versus Sullivan is that the press has a privilege to report matters of legitimate public interest even though such reports might intrude on matters otherwise private and then they go on. Excuse me, this holding refers to it. Time and Hill, then. Pardon? Doesn't that refer to Time and Hill? Yes, Your Honor. Yes, it does. The effect of that holding and of Sullivan. Yes, Your Honor. Excuse me. Then it goes on to analogize the reasoning and to say that the rights as enunciated, which give privilege of freedom of speech, freedom of the press, freedom to speak out on issues that are public, and in the dissent, in the Gertz case, it was pointed out, believed by Mr. Justice White, that he would have found differently because this was a comment upon a judicial proceeding so that all of the privilege that has been granted has been granted so far to expression, first of all, about public officials and then in Hill about an event of public interest, which is the opening of a new play. Then we go to the Butts case involving a football coach and to General Walker's speaking out on public issues. This bears no resemblance, I submit, to a matter like we have here. This is a private individual, a private citizen, who has certainly subjected himself to criticism by the press. I think that he stands in the same shoes as General Walker or any other entertainer. Suppose in the two syllabi, two and three, there had been a final phrase on there, under Ohio law, under two and three. Well, I don't, I don't think, Your Honor, that this would have... Well, you admit that two is under Ohio law. Yes, this is, this is a tort created by, as a common law right in Ohio. And you say three, also under Ohio law, a TV station has the privilege to report. Where would you be there? Well, if, I think we would be in the exact same position we are now, and that is... There would be no federal question, would there? I think there would be. I think there would be, Your Honor, because behind that syllabus, syllabus two and three, still lies the facts and circumstances and the reasoning, the express reasoning of the court. We can't reject that. I assume, I assume that Mr. Justice Marshall's question presupposed that you wouldn't have that material on page 13 that explicated the federal aspect. I think if they, if there was a, no reliance, whatever, on the First Amendment, then we wouldn't have the question that we have here. And that's exactly what you had in Gertz. On page 330 of the opinion in Gertz, they said, this case is here because the petitioner contests the applicability of the First Amendment to the facts and circumstances of Mr. Gertz. Do you get some support from your position from that footnote 5 at the bottom of page 14? The gravamen of the issue in this case is not whether the degree of intrusion is reasonable, but whether First Amendment principles require that the right of privacy give way to the public right to be informed of matters of public interest and concern and the concept of privilege seems to be, seems the more useful and appropriate one. Yes. I think that... You said that the syllabus may be illumined by the opinion. Yes. Yes, Your Honor. Under your law. Yes. And so that, may you rely on footnote 5? Yes, as part of the opinion, Your Honor, yes, we may. Let me pose a hypothetical to you and I'm going to ask your friends to comment on the same hypothetical later on when this turn comes. When Muhammad Ali engages in one of his professional exhibitions of prize fighting, I understand that the ratio is about 10 to 1 or more that the TV rights are many, many times the income he receives from the persons who are present at the arena. suppose surreptitiously either one of the networks or an outlaw group filmed the entire fight and then tried to put it on the air. Do you analogize your client's situation to what that would be with Muhammad Ali? Yes, I do, Your Honor. I feel that... Do you assume that you have TV rights to your client? I don't know that for a fact, Your Honor. Well, Muhammad Ali does. Well, I'm sure that he does. In fact, as a legal proposition he does, whether he does, whether he has some program for that, I don't know. But I think that it would be the very same situation if on a program on fine arts the media would go into the concert hall and tape the 8th Symphony, which Beethoven's 8th Symphony doesn't take more than a half an hour, and play the entire symphony. The difference is our case is stronger because Hugo Zucchini only has one performance. He doesn't play any different tune like a violinist. He has one 15-second act. And they have captured that over his specific objection, which I think is very important. Now, it has been stated that this is a limited privilege, but under the statement made in the Supreme Court... How was his objection made in advance? I lost track of it. There was an affidavit and the freelance TV photographer came out and asked him if he could film his act. And Mr. Zucchini said no. Before he did it, I see. Before he did it. And then the reporter went back and discussed this with his superiors. And the superiors apparently said, or the affidavit states in substance, go back and do it. And he did surreptitiously do that. Well, surreptitiously, but wasn't it in a public place to which no admission was charged? Yes. Yes. But he did it this time without permission and over the specific objections. And I mean that he did not get his permission when he went back again. I suppose, but if no permission was necessary to be there, say he'd never asked to do it, presumably he could have done it without anybody objecting and nothing surreptitious or off the record about it. Is it any different from doing something in a public park? I think you've already answered that. That's right. I think it's the same. I just point out that here there was... The objection really has no legal significance in the case. I think it makes a stronger case because the right as it may be defined, the right of the press as it may be defined is to act in a reasonable and responsible fashion in fulfilling their obligation to report news. I think when you can establish that they go beyond that. Now here, I do want to point out that in the third syllabus, this is described as a limited privilege. I don't think it is. They have the right to report in their newscasts matters otherwise privileged unless it's for a non-privileged use. Well, once you establish it is on a news program, it cannot be for a non-news use. The Supreme Court of Ohio would have reached a different result in your example of the taping of the eighth symphony played at Kennedy Center. The Ohio Supreme Court would not have. Even though that were put on an educational television station and not billed as news, but just said, you know, here's a brand new performance of Beethoven's A's. Well, I think if it was outside of a news showing, the Supreme Court of Ohio may very well have come to a different conclusion. But what they have said relates to news programs, as I read the third syllabus, rules, and that the only exception is when it is a non-news use, which seems to me to be a non-sequitur. You can't have, you can't fit into the right that the press gets under the First Amendment by the Supreme Court by putting it on your news if it's a non-news use. In other words, did he have a contract to perform? At the Burton County, at the Burton Fair? Yes, he did, Your Honor. But I gather from what your Supreme Court said at page 15, no issue of disregard of contract rights is involved here. That's right. There's no factual... This is just purely whether or not this was the report of a news event or the appropriation of a right. Under the contract, I assume he was paid. I presume he was. And that's critical, I suppose, to the Supreme Court, to the Ohio rule of a right of the publicity. If Mr. Zucchini had just done this for the fun of it, in the county park or in the public square or in his backyard, just like to do it every now and then. And a news camera had gone out there and reported that as news, there would be no proprietary right that had been appropriated, would there? Because he wouldn't have... Certainly no monetary right. I don't think that you would be able to establish any damages under Ohio law because he would have no commercial value if he did not perform as a professional entertainer. This was a property right for which he was paid. That's correct. contract. And that is critical, isn't it? Yes, it is. He is a professional entertainer and that's to whom the right applies. The right of publicity applies to an entertainer or to a professional athlete or to anyone who has developed some commercial value in the use of their name and their image and their success. performed in the square in front of the TV station for the general public to see. If he voluntarily performed in front of the TV cameras and knew that he was going to be put on the program, I think that that would be a different factual situation. Go ahead. Because he would... Leave out all you're adding to my question and answer it. If he performs in front of the TV station in a public square, can the TV station photograph it and put it on the news program? I don't think they could film his entire act. It's right in their backyard. It's different than doing it in his front yard. If he was doing it as a commercial act and TV cameras were there... If he was doing it and he was being paid because as he got shut out the camera, he had Bob Blatt's beer on the back. Could they publish that? No, I don't think they could publish his entire act under any circumstances. If he shot it into the TV window, could they do it then? Yes. I think that would be an exception because... The difference is that it's not his performance anymore, Mr. Justice Marshall. It is then an untoward event as the event that I suggested in my brief where he would miss the net and break his legs. Then I think it becomes something different than his professional act. It is no longer his professional act because something untoward has occurred. So I think that that's a different situation. In light of your colloquy with my brother Stuart, would you mind looking at A15? A15, what's the significance of the last sentence in that carryover paragraph? It might also be the case that the press would be liable if it recklessly disregarded contract rights existing between the plaintiff and a third person to present the performance to the public, but that question is not presented here. No, I'm sorry, page A? Page A15. A15. It's the last sentence in that carryover paragraph just before the last paragraph of the opinion. I take it that they're referring to the fact that if there was a contract between Mr. Zucchini and the persons who hired him, that his act was not to be filmed, that it would raise a different question, but that's not the question raised here. He doesn't have to go to take the trouble to exclude people. You're on the theory of your case, only the those can take the television pictures who have paid for that right, who have contracted with him for that, or contracted with the county. To film his entire act, I believe he would have to give permission. He would have to give them permission. That's what Muhammad Ali does, makes a separate contract. He doesn't rely on chance. He makes a separate contract for the television rights. That's especially necessary in his case, I would think. The other point I wanted to make about the so-called limited privilege was that they have accepted a news media presentation with actual intent to harm. And I think that that is also without any effect, because in this case, there was specific objection and they put his act on anyhow. And therefore, I don't know how they... wind up the showing, though, and you really can't appreciate this on TV. Go see it. Yes, they did. You have to see it, really, to appreciate it. Yes, they did. But I don't know how the court could ever expect anyone to establish intent to harm if intent to harm is not established by the newspaper, the news media people putting this on their show after he has objected. I think that the standards, as they have been enumerated in Time, in New York Times, and Hill, and further in Gertz, especially, and in Firestone, should not be applied to the right of publicity. I don't think there is any logic to it. I don't think there's any similarity to capturing an entire entertainer's performance and putting it on a news program. Thank you. Mr. Bryan. Mr. Chief Justice, and if the court please, I still am perplexed after hearing my eminent opponent here really as to how we got here. When I first heard that certiorari had been granted in this case, I was at least seriously puzzled, and as a matter of fact, had the apocryphal thought that perhaps we had slipped back to the looking glass of Lewis Carroll with Alice. Now, the explanations this morning in answering the court's questions get us no place, as it seems to me, either as to fundamental facts or fundamental law that raises a serious federal question that should be here. In the factual area, there is emphasis on the originality of an artist's act and that sort of thing. There is a book on circus that was written quite a few years ago. It's a historical authority, apparently, on the subject by Marianne Murray. And in that book, great credit is given to the zucchinis as inventors, as trapeze artists, as writers. And one of the things that first got them to notice in this country was the invention of a better mechanism for a canon to project a human being by Hugo's father and his brother. And Hugo was the first man who did it, apparently, with that mechanism a better one. But P.T. Barnum shot Mademoiselle Zazel out of a cannon for 60 feet back in 1879 and called it the Human Cannonball Act. Well, there's nothing very original about the performances of the Eighth Symphony, but do you suggest that if someone came in and covered it at Kennedy Center without the consent of the performers, the conductor, and the members of the orchestra, they could put it on television? No, sir. And I don't think that this... Well, then what's the history of the act got to do with it? I don't see how this theory of a unique little situation of a 15-second act can apply on any broad principle to the kind of question that you're raising, sir. Well, what's the difference whether it takes 15 seconds or 30 minutes for the performance? It would make a serious difference under the definition of the media privilege by the Ohio Supreme Court. They have said that the media may use it in the news contents, but they may not appropriate the benefit of the publicity for some non-privileged private use. You can't make a news program, in my judgment, that's going to stand up in the Court of Ohio in the face of that, out of a full symphony. Well, that wouldn't be a non-privileged private use. It would be a use on the news program, precisely the same use as was made of the Cannonball Act here, wouldn't it? In the hypothetical question. It wouldn't be a private use. Mr. Justice Stewart, I don't see how we are going to be able to conceive that the entire long performances of those people who are protecting themselves. They are protected by the notice on the ticket. There are contract arrangements that are made, and performers like Mr. Zucchini enter into contracts with people at fairs, at the ballpark when they put on acts. They have contracts which limit the right of anybody to come in and take it. And I would say that in answer to the question that Mr. Chief Justice asked about Muhammad Ali, that there isn't any possibility, in my judgment, that that would get by the state of Ohio. The state of Ohio is not saying you can go in and steal things and break contracts. Well, some of Mr. Muhammad Ali's performances last only about 15 seconds. Does that mean that the performance would be open to any surreptitious coverage by a television camera? This was not surreptitious. Well. That the TV people along with others were invited free in order to do this, and my eminent colleague... Not by Mr. Zucchini, though. No, but he contracted to put on a performance for some promoters who did invite these people, and he did not have an agreement with them, that they would prevent the taking of pictures. And as a matter of fact, the only facts in this record do not support my eminent counsel's position with respect to the matter of how the Zucchini seeking out the photographer and objecting. There is an affidavit. Mr. Bryan, before you get into that factual point of your preceding remark in response to the Chief Justice, as to a different rule obtaining in Ohio if the promoters had excluded the TV people, it's my impression that, at least your colleague contends, that the Supreme Court of Ohio felt constrained to reach the result it did here because of the First Amendment. That is, that we're not judging Ohio's choice of policies, but that Ohio might have produced a different result here had it not been for the First Amendment. Well, Mr. Justice Rehnquist, I cannot find that doubt in what the Court did. Now, if this Court does find it, then I think the proper approach would be to ask the Ohio Supreme Court. The funny thing about all this relying on the... Mr. Bryan, pardon? What about what I read your colleague from footnote 5? I beg your pardon, Mr. Justice Rehnquist. What about what appears in footnote 5, that the grovelment of the issue in this case is not whether the degree of intrusion is reasonable, but whether First Amendment principles require that the right of privacy give way to the public right to be informed of matters of public interest and concern? Well, absolutely, and from the point of view of free speech... No, no, I'm addressing what you just said, that there's no First Amendment to share. All they say is that there is a principle involved here. That's what they were seeking, and that footnote is in connection with their seeking, and I was going to go into exactly what they sought and found very briefly. But you say what they did was fashion a state rule, even though under the influence of First Amendment principles, is that what you're saying? Well, absolutely, Your Honor.
